extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, law students, policymakers, and stakeholders in software-related patents
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101 for computer-implemented inventions, with focus on the abstract-ideas exception and related tests (e.g., method-or-means, 'significantly more'). Useful for evaluating whether claims to methods, systems, or computer-readable media are eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of patent-eligible subject matter (§101)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four categories of patent-eligible subject matter: processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter; these categories should be read broadly to encourage innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be evaluated to determine whether they fall within one of these statutory categories (e.g., method patents, data processing systems, computer-readable media). Being in a statutory category is a necessary starting point but not alone dispositive because judicial exceptions may still apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court has recognized three exceptions to patentable subject matter under §101: laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing eligibility, first identify whether a claim is directed to one of these exceptions; if so, proceed to analyze whether the claim claims more than the exception in a way that renders it patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas exception — core inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to an 'abstract idea' (e.g., fundamental truths, mathematical formulas, or fundamental economic concepts such as intermediated settlement or hedging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed subject matter is essentially a longstanding practice or fundamental economic principle (CLS's position) or instead claims a specific technical application beyond a preexisting fundamental truth (Alice's position). Look to precedent (e.g., Bilski) for examples of abstract economic concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-or-means test (method/means vs. effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent should be granted for the method or means of producing a beneficial effect but not for the effect itself (the method or means test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim merely asserts the beneficial result (the effect) without claiming a concrete method or means of achieving it, it is likely unpatentable; example given: Pythagorean theorem explains a relation but does not cause it and thus is unpatentable in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Significantly more" / inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that involve a judicial exception (like an abstract idea) must add 'significantly more' than the exception itself (as articulated in Mayo) to be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the claim recites an inventive concept or additional elements that transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (e.g., Diamond v. Diehr: combination of steps plus a formula was eligible). Mere recital of an abstract idea plus routine steps is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere computer implementation ('do it on a computer') is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing an abstract idea on a computer, or adding conventional computer functions ('compute it', electronic recordkeeping), does not by itself make an abstract idea patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that simply instruct 'do X using a computer' or claim basic functions of computers are likely to be treated as claiming the abstract idea itself; courts look for non-conventional, non-generic computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-solution activity is insufficient to confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that only add insignificant 'post-solution activity' to an abstract idea (i.e., steps that occur after application of a law/idea) do not render the claim patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to precedent (Bilski, Mayo) where post-solution activity was considered inadequate; evaluate whether claimed steps are integral inventive steps or merely post-hoc additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern (do not tie up foundational tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims should not preempt the use of basic tools of scientific and technological work (i.e., take from the public necessary foundational tools for innovation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether allowing the claim would prevent others from using fundamental concepts (e.g., economic practices, mathematical relationships) that are basic building blocks for further innovation; preemption is a key policy consideration against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific, concrete configurations or non-conventional steps support eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that require a specific configuration of computer hardware or particular, concrete steps (e.g., creating two shadow accounts, a particular series of steps beyond simple computations) may demonstrate the 'significantly more' needed for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for claim elements that meaningfully limit the scope in a technological way (novel hardware arrangement, novel sequence of steps producing a technical effect) rather than generic computer implementation; such specificity can distinguish from 'disembodied concept' claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of computer-readable media claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to computer-readable media containing program code are evaluated for §101 eligibility and can be found ineligible if they are directed at the same abstract concept as method/system claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume drafting as a media claim avoids §101 problems; analyze whether the media claim simply recites the abstract idea in software form without adding an inventive application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining whether a claim 'recites a fundamental truth' or is reducible to a formula
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is more likely to be an abstract idea if it merely recites a fundamental truth or is reducible to a mathematical formula or preexisting principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the claimed subject matter exists apart from human action or is a longstanding/prior commercial practice; if so, courts may find it falls within the abstract-ideas exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of precedent (Bilski, Mayo, Diehr) in eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior Supreme Court decisions provide tests and examples (Bilski: hedging as abstract idea; Mayo: 'significantly more'; Diehr: combinated process including formula was eligible) that guide §101 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply tests and analogies from these cases: compare claimed invention to prior holdings (is it like hedging or like Diehr's integrated process?) to determine whether the claim adds an inventive application beyond an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for clarity and consistent framework in applying the abstract-ideas exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower courts currently face uncertainty applying the abstract ideas exception; commentators urge the Court to clarify standards or emphasize tests (e.g., method-and-means) to provide consistent guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing claims, be explicit about which test is applied (abstract-idea identification, then whether the claim adds 'significantly more' or a method/means) and document how each claim element affects the analysis to reduce uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy balancing: encouraging innovation vs. preventing undue monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analysis should consider policy effects: broad eligibility can encourage investment in early-stage software innovations, while overbroad patents can hinder competition by monopolizing fundamental concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh whether granting a patent will meaningfully promote progress in useful arts (Constitutional purpose) versus whether it would improperly reward mere idea conception or block follow-on innovation; amici arguments reflect these policy tensions.
